section.title: The Brothers Go to Egypt
section.sectionRationale: The famine that Joseph foresaw now drives his brothers to the very man they betrayed. Without knowing it, they bow before the brother they sold, and his dreams begin to come true. The chapter turns from grain to guilt, as an old sin surfaces in a foreign court.
section.thesis: God uses famine and a hidden ruler to bring the guilty brothers low, awakening their consciences and setting in motion the reconciliation that will save the family alive.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: Jacob sends his sons for grain; they bow before Joseph and are accused; a buried guilt is awakened; and dread deepens as the silver is found and Jacob refuses to risk Benjamin.

units.label: Sent down to Egypt
units.note: so that we may live and not die

verses.text: When Jacob learned that there was grain in Egypt, he said to his sons, “Why are you staring at one another?”
“Look,” he added, “I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy some for us, so that we may live and not die.”
So ten of Joseph’s brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt.
But Jacob did not send Joseph’s brother Benjamin with his brothers, for he said, “I am afraid that harm might befall him.”
So the sons of Israel were among those who came to buy grain, since the famine had also spread to the land of Canaan.

units.label: Bowing before the brother they sold
units.note: Joseph's dreams begin to come true

verses.text: Now Joseph was the ruler of the land; he was the one who sold grain to all its people. So when his brothers arrived, they bowed down before him with their faces to the ground.

And when Joseph saw his brothers, he recognized them, but he treated them as strangers and spoke harshly to them. “Where have you come from?” he asked. “From the land of Canaan,” they replied. “We are here to buy food.”
Although Joseph recognized his brothers, they did not recognize him.
Joseph remembered his dreams about them and said, “You are {{ragal|spies}}! You have come to see if our land is vulnerable.”
“Not so, my lord,” they replied. “Your servants have come to buy food.
We are all sons of one man. Your servants are honest men, not spies.”
“No,” he told them. “You have come to see if our land is vulnerable.”
But they answered, “Your servants are twelve brothers, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan. The youngest is now with our father, and one is no more.”
Then Joseph declared, “Just as I said, you are spies!
And this is how you will be {{bachan|tested}}: As surely as Pharaoh lives, you shall not leave this place unless your youngest brother comes here.
Send one of your number to get your brother; the rest of you will be confined so that the truth of your words may be tested. If they are untrue, then as surely as Pharaoh lives, you are spies!”
So Joseph imprisoned them for three days,

units.label: A guilty conscience awakened
units.note: surely we are being punished because of our brother

verses.text: and on the third day he said to them, “I fear God. So do this and you will live:
If you are honest, leave one of your brothers in custody while the rest of you go and take back grain to relieve the hunger of your households.
Then bring your youngest brother to me so that your words can be verified, that you may not die.” And to this they consented.
Then they said to one another, “Surely we are being punished because of our brother. We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we would not listen. That is why this distress has come upon us.”
And Reuben responded, “Didn’t I tell you not to sin against the boy? But you would not listen. Now we must account for his blood!”
They did not realize that Joseph understood them, since there was an interpreter between them.
And he turned away from them and wept. When he turned back and spoke to them, he took Simeon from them and had him bound before their eyes.
Then Joseph gave orders to fill their bags with grain, to return each man’s silver to his sack, and to give them provisions for their journey. This order was carried out,
and they loaded the grain on their donkeys and departed.
At the place where they lodged for the night, one of them opened his sack to get feed for his donkey, and he saw his silver in the mouth of the sack.
“My silver has been returned!” he said to his brothers. “It is here in my sack.” Their hearts sank, and trembling, they turned to one another and said, “What is this that God has done to us?”
When they reached their father Jacob in the land of Canaan, they described to him all that had happened to them:
“The man who is lord of the land spoke harshly to us and accused us of spying on the country.
But we told him, ‘We are honest men, not spies.
We are twelve brothers, sons of one father. One is no more, and the youngest is now with our father in the land of Canaan.’
Then the man who is lord of the land said to us, ‘This is how I will know whether you are honest: Leave one brother with me, take food to relieve the hunger of your households, and go.
But bring your youngest brother back to me so I will know that you are not spies but honest men. Then I will give your brother back to you, and you can trade in the land.’”
As they began emptying their sacks, there in each man’s sack was his bag of silver! And when they and their father saw the bags of silver, they were dismayed.
Their father Jacob said to them, “You have deprived me of my sons. Joseph is gone and Simeon is no more. Now you want to take Benjamin. Everything is going against me!”
Then Reuben said to his father, “You may kill my two sons if I fail to bring him back to you. Put him in my care, and I will return him.”

But Jacob replied, “My son will not go down there with you, for his brother is dead, and he alone is left. If any harm comes to him on your journey, you will bring my gray hair down to {{sheol|Sheol}} in sorrow.”

ragal.gloss: To go about on foot, and so to spy out or scout. The accusation that they are spies is heavy with irony, for these men once schemed in secret against their own brother. Joseph presses the charge not out of cruelty but to test whether they have changed.

bachan.gloss: To test, examine, or prove, often as metal is assayed by fire. Joseph puts his brothers to the proof to see what is truly in their hearts. Scripture uses the same word for how God tests the righteous to reveal and refine them.

sheol.gloss: The grave or the realm of the dead, the place to which all the living descend. Jacob fears that losing Benjamin will send him grieving to Sheol. His words expose a father whose whole hope now rests on one remaining son of Rachel.

basic.context: The famine Joseph predicted has reached Canaan, so Jacob sends ten sons to buy grain in Egypt. There they bow before the governor without knowing he is the brother they sold years before. The key question is whether God is simply punishing them or quietly working to restore them.
basic.hermeneutics: This is narrative, and it moves by dramatic irony: we know who Joseph is, but the brothers do not. The main question is why Joseph tests them so severely rather than revealing himself at once. The answer unfolds as we watch old guilt rise to the surface.
basic.originalLanguages: The charge that they are spies, from a word for scouting on foot, is loaded with irony against men who once plotted in secret. Joseph tests them, a word used for assaying metal, to see their hearts. Jacob speaks of going down to Sheol, the grave, if he loses another son.
basic.typology: Joseph, the rejected brother now raised to power, holds the fate of those who wronged him and yet weeps for them. This points forward to Christ, the brother His own people rejected, exalted to hold the bread of life and moved with compassion for the guilty.
basic.christ: Joseph turns aside to weep even while he tests them, and he is the only source of grain in the land. So Jesus, rejected by His brothers, becomes the one to whom all must come for bread, and He receives sinners with tears rather than vengeance.
basic.god: God is at work behind the famine, the journey, and even the returned silver. The brothers sense His hand and ask, what is this that God has done to us. He is bringing hidden sin into the light so that it can finally be healed.
basic.crossReferences: Their bowing fulfills Joseph's dreams in Genesis 37. Their awakened guilt echoes the sin recorded there, and Joseph's later words in Genesis 50:20 interpret the whole account: what they meant for evil, God meant for good.
basic.oneStory: This is the beginning of the family's rescue. God preserves the line of promise through famine by the very brother they tried to destroy, keeping alive the people from whom the Saviour will come.

context.literary:
Genesis 42 moves in a round trip: out from Canaan, verses 1 to 5; the encounter in Egypt, verses 6 to 24; and back to Canaan, verses 25 to 38. The journey home is not a return to where things were. The brothers go down ten and come back nine, their silver is back in their sacks, and the weight of an old sin has come back with it.

The chapter is written as a deliberate echo of Genesis 37, and almost every detail rhymes with the day Joseph was sold. There the brothers put Joseph in a pit; here they are put in custody, verse 17. There they sold him for silver, Genesis 37:28; here silver keeps turning up where it should not be, verses 27 and 35. There Reuben tried to save the boy, Genesis 37:21-22; here Reuben says, 'Didn't I tell you?' verse 22. There they asked their father to 'examine' a bloodied robe; here they are told to bring proof that their words are true. There a brother was 'gone'; here 'one is no more,' verses 13 and 32. There Jacob said he would go down to Sheol mourning, Genesis 37:35; here he fears his gray hair will go down to Sheol in sorrow, verse 38. The narrator is showing measure for measure: the brothers are being made to live through what they did.

The narrator also lets the reader into rooms the characters cannot enter. Only we know that Joseph remembered his dreams, verse 9, that he understood every word, verse 23, and that he turned away and wept, verse 24. Only in this chapter do we learn that Joseph had 'pleaded' with them from the pit, verse 21, a detail Genesis 37 held back until the brothers' own consciences supplied it.

The brothers' report to Jacob in verses 29 to 34 is also telling for what it leaves out. They do not mention the three days in prison, or that Simeon was bound before their eyes. They soften the story for their father, just as they once deceived him with the robe. Their habits have not yet fully changed.
context.historical:
The famine had 'spread to the land of Canaan,' verse 5, and the brothers are 'among those who came to buy grain,' part of a stream of foreigners arriving at Egypt's frontier. Egypt's reliance on the Nile rather than on rainfall meant that it could have grain when neighbouring lands had none, and Semitic groups from Canaan are known to have come to Egypt in times of hardship.

Egypt's northeastern border faced the routes from Canaan and was guarded against infiltration from Asia. A party of ten grown men from the same region, arriving together, might plausibly have been suspected of scouting. The charge that they had come 'to see if our land is vulnerable,' literally 'the nakedness of the land,' means spying out its undefended points.

The 'silver' of verses 25 to 35 was not coinage, which appeared many centuries later. Payment was made in weighed silver, often carried tied in a small bag or bundle, which is why each man finds 'his bag of silver' in his sack, verse 35. The discovery at the 'place where they lodged,' verse 27, a stopping point on the road, would have been terrifying: returned payment could look like theft and invite a charge of stealing from the lord of Egypt.

Joseph keeps 'an interpreter between them,' verse 23, which is natural for an Egyptian official addressing foreigners, and it preserves his disguise. His oath 'as surely as Pharaoh lives,' verses 15 and 16, is the kind of oath by the life of the king that an Egyptian official would swear. The whole chapter keeps Joseph wholly Egyptian in manner, so completely that his own brothers, who last saw him as a teenager, cannot see through it.
context.canonical:
The principle the brothers discover in this chapter is stated in the Law: 'be assured that your sin will find you out,' Numbers 32:23. It is also the experience David describes: 'When I kept silent, my bones became brittle,' until 'I acknowledged my sin to You,' Psalm 32:3-5. Proverbs puts it as a rule of life: 'He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy,' Proverbs 28:13. The brothers' long concealment is about to be broken open.

Reuben's words, 'Now we must account for his blood,' verse 22, reach back to God's word after the flood, 'I will demand an accounting from anyone who takes the life of his fellow man,' Genesis 9:5, and further back still to Abel, whose blood cried out from the ground, Genesis 4:10. The story of brothers who harm brothers began with Cain, and here that story is heading toward its fullest reconciliation in Genesis.

The later Scriptures remember this journey. Psalm 105:16 says God 'called down famine on the land,' making the hunger that drives this chapter His own act. Stephen distinguishes the two visits, 'When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers on their first visit. On their second visit, Joseph revealed his identity,' Acts 7:12-13, and draws a lesson from it: God's deliverers are often not recognised by their own people at first, Acts 7:25.

The pattern of famine driving a son back toward reconciliation appears again in Jesus' parable of the prodigal son, whose hunger in a far country brings him to his senses, Luke 15:17-20. The New Testament also names the kind of sorrow the brothers are beginning to feel: 'Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret,' 2 Corinthians 7:10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see how God deals with buried sin in His own people. The brothers who founded Israel's tribes were not heroes; they were men who had sold their brother and lied to their father for over twenty years. The chapter shows God neither ignoring their sin nor destroying them for it, but patiently bringing it to the surface where it can be confessed and healed.

He also meant his hearers to see that God's word to Joseph in his dreams could not be undone. The very act by which the brothers tried to end the dreams, selling Joseph, became the path by which they now bow before him. The first hearers were being taught to trust that no human scheme can overturn what God has spoken.

Finally, the author wanted Israel to notice that conscience is part of God's providence. Nothing in Joseph's words mentions their brother, yet the brothers immediately connect their distress with their old sin, verse 21, and by the end they are asking, 'What is this that God has done to us?' verse 28. God was working not only through famine and trade but in the hearts of guilty men, readying them for the mercy He was about to show.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This chapter describes Joseph's conduct; it does not commend every part of it as a model. His harsh speech, his false accusation that they are spies, and his secret return of their silver are recorded without comment. They serve a larger purpose in the story, but they do not give believers permission to deceive or manipulate those who have wronged them. The New Testament's instruction for those who have been wronged is clear: 'Do not avenge yourselves,' Romans 12:19, and 'Forgive as the Lord forgave you,' Colossians 3:13.

What does carry forward is the reality of conscience and repentance. The brothers' confession, 'we saw his anguish... but we would not listen,' verse 21, is a model of honest acknowledgment that names the sin without excuse. Their fear shows the burden of unconfessed guilt. And Joseph's goal, to discover whether his brothers had changed rather than to punish them, shows that true reconciliation may require truth to be faced before trust can be restored. Forgiveness is freely given, but restored relationship involves repentance.

debates.question: Why does Joseph conceal his identity and deal harshly with his brothers?

views.label: Testing toward repentance
views.case: Joseph is probing whether they have changed, especially toward Benjamin, the other son of Rachel, whom they might treat as they once treated him. His demand for Benjamin, his holding Simeon, and later the planted cup in chapter 44 all create situations that reveal their hearts. His tears in verse 24 show love, not revenge.

views.label: Working through his own pain
views.case: Some see Joseph also wrestling with old wounds. He 'remembered his dreams,' verse 9, and perhaps the pit; the harshness may reflect a real, unresolved history, and it takes him time before he can trust and forgive. The narrator's frequent notes about his weeping suggest a man under great inner strain.

views.label: Fulfilling the dreams
views.case: A few suggest that Joseph, remembering his dreams, sought to bring about their full fulfilment, which required all eleven brothers, and even his father, to bow before him, Genesis 37:9. That is why he insists that Benjamin must come.

debates.bearing: The text supports the first two readings together. Joseph is testing their hearts, and he is a wounded man doing it. Either way the goal is restoration, not retaliation, since he weeps rather than gloats and provides for them even while he tests them.

debates.question: Why does Joseph choose Simeon to be held in Egypt?

views.label: Because Reuben tried to save him
views.case: Joseph had just overheard Reuben say, 'Didn't I tell you not to sin against the boy?' verse 22. Learning for the first time that the eldest had opposed the plot, Joseph passes over Reuben and takes the next eldest, Simeon, who may have taken the lead in the violence.

views.label: Because of Simeon's character
views.case: Simeon, with Levi, had already slaughtered the men of Shechem, Genesis 34:25, and Jacob would later condemn their violence, Genesis 49:5-7. Some suggest that Simeon had been especially cruel toward Joseph, and that holding him would also separate the most dangerous brother from Benjamin.

debates.bearing: The text does not give Joseph's reason, so certainty is impossible. The first view has the advantage of following directly from verse 22. Either way the choice keeps one brother bound in Egypt, so that the others must decide whether to abandon a brother again.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's most skilful wordplay is in verse 7: 'Joseph saw his brothers, he recognized them, but he treated them as strangers.' Both verbs come from the same root, nakar. The first, wayyakirem, means 'he recognised them'; the second, wayyitnakker, means 'he made himself a stranger' or 'disguised himself.' Verse 8 repeats the root twice more: Joseph recognised them, they did not recognise him. Recognition is a thread through these chapters. The brothers asked Jacob to 'examine' the robe and Jacob 'recognized it,' Genesis 37:32-33; Tamar asked Judah to 'examine' the seal and cord and Judah 'recognized the items,' Genesis 38:25-26. The deceivers are now the ones who cannot see.

'Spies,' verse 9, is meraggelim, from the root ragal, related to regel, 'foot,' and meaning to go about on foot, to scout. It is the word used of Joshua's spies sent to Jericho, Joshua 2:1. The charge that they have come to see 'if our land is vulnerable' is literally to see 'the nakedness of the land,' 'ervat ha'arets. A land's nakedness is its undefended places. The men who once stripped their brother of his robe, Genesis 37:23, are accused of coming to see a land's nakedness.

The brothers keep insisting that they are 'honest men,' kenim, verses 11, 19, 31, 33 and 34. The word comes from ken, the ordinary Hebrew word for 'so' or 'right,' and it means men whose words match the facts. Its repetition is heavy with irony, since these men had lived a lie before their father for over twenty years.

Joseph says they will be 'tested,' verses 15 and 16, from bachan, a word used for the assaying of metals. Its theological use is striking: 'You, O God, have tested us; You have refined us like silver,' Psalm 66:10; 'I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind,' Jeremiah 17:10. Joseph's test is a human instrument of the divine testing of hearts.

The brothers' confession in verse 21 is carefully worded. 'Surely we are being punished' reads more literally, 'Truly we are guilty,' using the root 'asham, the word that later names the guilt offering in Leviticus. Then comes a wordplay: 'We saw his anguish,' tsarat nafsho, the distress of his soul, and 'That is why this distress,' hatstsarah, 'has come upon us.' His distress has become theirs. Joseph 'pleaded' with them, hitchanan, a form of the verb chanan, 'to be gracious,' meaning to beg for mercy. In Genesis 43:29 Joseph will bless Benjamin with the same root: 'May God be gracious to you.' The one who begged for grace will be the one who gives it.

Reuben's 'Now we must account for his blood' is literally 'his blood is being required,' from darash, the verb God uses in Genesis 9:5, 'I will demand an accounting.' And the 'interpreter' of verse 23 is melits, a go-between, the word Elihu uses when he longs for 'one mediator in a thousand,' Job 33:23. The brothers think a mediator stands between them and the lord of the land. In fact the lord of the land is their brother, and he understands every word.

typology.type: The rejected brother, unrecognised by his own
typology.fulfillment: Joseph stands before his brothers as lord of the land, and 'they did not recognize him,' verse 8. John writes of Christ, 'He was in the world, and though the world was made through Him, the world did not recognize Him. He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him,' John 1:10-11. Peter tells the crowds in Jerusalem that they acted in ignorance, Acts 3:17, and many were 'cut to the heart,' Acts 2:37, as the brothers are pierced by conscience in verse 21. The type falls short in that Joseph hid himself deliberately, while Christ openly declared who He was, and the failure to recognise Him lay entirely with those who would not see.

typology.type: The sole keeper of the grain
typology.fulfillment: Joseph was 'the one who sold grain to all its people,' verse 6. Those who needed life had nowhere else to go, and they had to come to the very brother they had rejected. So with Christ: 'Salvation exists in no one else,' Acts 4:12, and the stone the builders rejected is the one through whom life is given. The correspondence is that sinners must come for life to the One they wronged. The escalation is that Christ does not merely sell bread that sustains the body; He is the bread of life, John 6:35, and gives Himself.

typology.type: Tears hidden behind a stern face
typology.fulfillment: Joseph speaks harshly, binds Simeon before their eyes, and yet 'he turned away from them and wept,' verse 24. His severity serves his love. Jesus wept over Jerusalem even while He pronounced judgment on it, Luke 19:41-44, and His rebukes to Peter served his restoration, as when He asked three times, 'Do you love Me?' and Peter was deeply hurt, John 21:17. The type falls short because Joseph's tears were hidden and mixed with his own wounds, whereas Christ's compassion is perfect and open, and He is 'able to sympathize with our weaknesses,' Hebrews 4:15.

Joseph orders that each man's silver be returned in his sack, verse 25. The grain has in effect been given freely, but the brothers cannot receive it as a gift; they tremble and ask what God has done to them, verse 28. The gospel offers what the brothers could not yet grasp: sinners are 'justified freely by His grace,' Romans 3:24, and invited to 'buy, and eat' without money, Isaiah 55:1. The type shows how guilt makes grace look like a trap. It falls short because Joseph's gift was hidden and part of a test, while God's grace in Christ is openly proclaimed.

study.christ:
Genesis 42 leads to Christ first by the pattern of the rejected brother who holds the bread of life. The brothers had cast Joseph out, and now they must come to him for grain, bowing with faces to the ground, verse 6. The New Testament tells the same story of Jesus: 'He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him,' John 1:11. Yet the one who was rejected is the only one through whom life comes, and 'Salvation exists in no one else,' Acts 4:12.

It leads to Christ by the pattern of hidden identity leading to recognition. The brothers stood before Joseph and did not know him. Peter's sermon at Pentecost confronts Jerusalem with the fact that the Jesus they crucified is Lord and Christ, and the hearers 'were cut to the heart and asked Peter and the other apostles, "Brothers, what shall we do?"' Acts 2:37. Zechariah foresaw the day when Israel would 'look on Me, the One they have pierced' and mourn, Zechariah 12:10. Joseph's brothers are the first in Scripture to discover that the one they wronged is the one who holds their future.

It leads to Christ by the way severity serves love. Joseph's harsh words and his testing of the brothers aim at their restoration, not their ruin, and in the middle of it he turns away and weeps, verse 24. Jesus deals with sinners in the same spirit. His hard sayings aim at repentance, and 'God's kindness leads you to repentance,' Romans 2:4. After Peter's denial Jesus did not simply pass over the failure; He asked three times, 'Do you love Me?' until Peter was grieved, and then restored him, John 21:15-17. Truth faced leads to love restored.

It leads to Christ by contrast in the matter of the mediator. The brothers speak to Joseph through an interpreter, verse 23, never guessing that the man across the table understands them perfectly. Christ is the true Mediator, who needs no one to tell Him what is in the human heart, John 2:25, and who stands not between us and a stranger but between us and the Father as our Brother, 'not ashamed to call them brothers,' Hebrews 2:11.

A caution is needed. Joseph is a real man with real faults, and not everything he does is a picture of Christ. His deceptions belong to his own story, and it would be forced to make every detail, the sacks, the donkeys, the lodging place, into a hidden message. The link to Christ lies in the larger pattern that Stephen himself saw: God's appointed deliverer is first rejected by his brothers, then becomes the one to whom they must come, Acts 7:9-13. In Christ that pattern reaches its end. The Brother we rejected stands ready to receive us, and His tears come before His self-revelation.
study.god:
This chapter shows God working almost entirely behind the scenes. His name is spoken only twice, once by Joseph, 'I fear God,' verse 18, and once by the brothers in dread, 'What is this that God has done to us?' verse 28. Yet the reader knows that God has sent the famine, Psalm 105:16, directed the brothers to Egypt and brought them before the very man they betrayed. The doctrine of providence is here in narrative form. God governs hunger, trade, travel and the timing of a single meeting, and He does it through ordinary causes.

God is shown to be just. The brothers are made to taste what they gave. They are confined, as they confined Joseph; they are accused falsely, as they lied about him; they are threatened with the loss of a brother, as they caused the loss of one. The chapter illustrates a principle of divine justice that Scripture states elsewhere, 'be assured that your sin will find you out,' Numbers 32:23. God does not let buried sin stay buried forever.

Yet God's justice here is the servant of His mercy. The purpose of this reckoning is not to destroy the brothers but to bring them to confession. They leave with grain for their families and their silver returned. God wounds in order to heal. As Hebrews says of God's discipline, 'Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it,' Hebrews 12:11.

God is also the God of conscience. No one in Egypt mentions Joseph, yet the brothers immediately trace their distress to 'our brother,' verse 21. God's law is written on the heart, and He can awaken memory and guilt without a word being spoken. 'The LORD is the tester of hearts,' Proverbs 17:3.

The chapter holds a real tension in Jacob's lament: 'Everything is going against me!' verse 36. From where Jacob stands, God's providence looks like loss upon loss. The reader knows that Joseph is alive, Simeon is safe and the whole family is about to be saved. God's ways often look most like defeat just before they are revealed as deliverance. Paul gives the answer Jacob could not yet see: 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' Romans 8:31.

Finally, Joseph's words 'I fear God' tell us something about God through His servant. The fear of God is the ground of justice and mercy among people. Abraham once feared there was 'no fear of God in this place,' Genesis 20:11; the Hebrew midwives 'feared God' and let the boys live, Exodus 1:17. Because Joseph fears God, the brothers are shown mercy they did not deserve.

For worship, the chapter invites believers to trust God's hand in hard providences, to let Him bring hidden sin to light rather than hiding it, and to know that His severity toward His people is always in the service of their restoration.

crossReferences.note: Joseph's boyhood dreams of sheaves and stars bowing to him. In Genesis 42:6 the brothers bow before him 'with their faces to the ground,' using the same verb, and verse 9 says that Joseph 'remembered his dreams about them.' The dream begins to come true.

Reuben tried to save Joseph, urging the brothers not to shed his blood. In Genesis 42:22 he reminds them, 'Didn't I tell you not to sin against the boy?' Overhearing this may be why Joseph passes over Reuben and binds Simeon.

Judah proposed selling Joseph, and they sold him for twenty shekels of silver. In chapter 42 the silver keeps coming back, found in the mouth of each man's sack, until the brothers tremble, a haunting reminder of the silver they once took for their brother.

Jacob refused to be comforted and said he would go down to Sheol mourning for Joseph. In Genesis 42:38 he uses the same picture for Benjamin, 'you will bring my gray hair down to Sheol in sorrow,' showing that the old wound is still open.

God says, 'I will demand an accounting from anyone who takes the life of his fellow man.' Reuben's 'we must account for his blood,' Genesis 42:22, uses the same verb, darash. The brothers recognise that shedding a brother's blood, or selling him to his likely death, puts them under God's reckoning.

'Be assured that your sin will find you out.' Moses' warning to the tribes describes exactly what happens in Genesis 42. More than twenty years after the sale of Joseph, the brothers' sin rises to meet them in a foreign court, not through any accusation but through God's providence and their own consciences.

David describes the misery of hidden sin, bones wasting away, until he confessed and was forgiven. The brothers' confession in Genesis 42:21, 'we saw his anguish... but we would not listen,' is the first crack in a long silence, the beginning of the path David describes.

Stephen distinguishes the brothers' two visits: on the first they did not know Joseph; 'on their second visit, Joseph revealed his identity.' Stephen tells the story to show that Israel has always failed to recognise the deliverer God sends, which the council was doing again with Jesus.

'He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him.' As the brothers did not recognise Joseph though he stood before them, so Christ was not recognised by His own people. In both stories the rejected one holds the life that the rejecters need.

In Jesus' parable a famine drives the younger son back to his father, confessing, 'I have sinned.' Famine drives Jacob's sons to Egypt, where their guilt surfaces. In both stories hunger becomes God's instrument for bringing the guilty to repentance and home.

'Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret.' The brothers' grief in Genesis 42:21 is the beginning of such sorrow, not mere fear of punishment but an honest naming of what they did to their brother. It will ripen into Judah's self-offering in chapter 44.

Joseph's final interpretation of the whole story: 'what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good... to preserve the lives of many people.' Genesis 42 is where the brothers first begin to discover that their evil has been taken up into God's purpose.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 42 answers a question that runs from the first family of Genesis. Ever since Cain rose against Abel, Genesis 4:8, brothers in Genesis have hurt brothers: Ishmael and Isaac, Esau and Jacob, and now the ten and Joseph. God asked Cain, 'Where is your brother Abel?' Genesis 4:9, and the ten have been silent for over twenty years about their brother. The fall did not only break humanity's relationship with God; it broke brotherhood. Jacob and Esau embraced, Genesis 33:4, but this chapter begins the fullest story of reconciliation in Genesis, one that reaches down to confession and forgiveness.

It also carries forward the promise to Abraham in the face of death. The famine threatens the very family through whom all nations are to be blessed. God preserves it, not by a miracle in Canaan, but by sending them down to Egypt, to the brother they rejected, who now holds the grain. The descent to Egypt that God foretold to Abraham, Genesis 15:13, is starting, and its end will be the Exodus.

The chapter sets up the next movements. Simeon is left bound in Egypt; Benjamin is demanded; Jacob refuses. The family is at an impasse that only a change of heart can break, and in chapter 43 Judah will step forward, and in chapter 44 he will offer himself in Benjamin's place. God is using the pressure of famine to form a new character in the family of promise.

In the whole sweep of Scripture the pattern of this chapter becomes the pattern of the gospel. The Son whom His brothers rejected is exalted, and those who rejected Him must come to Him for life. Peter's hearers at Pentecost, like Joseph's brothers, discover to their horror that the one they wronged is Lord, and to their joy that He receives them. Through the cross Christ reconciles estranged peoples 'to God in one body,' Ephesians 2:16.

The new creation will be a family fully reconciled. The tears Joseph weeps in secret, and the grief Jacob carries to the edge of Sheol, will be answered when 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,' Revelation 21:4. The brothers who once could not speak a kind word to Joseph will, in the end, eat at his table, and the people of God from every nation will sit together at the table of the Lamb.

quiz.q: What happens when the brothers arrive before the governor of Egypt?

options.text: They bow with their faces to the ground, unknowingly fulfilling Joseph's dreams.
options.note: Their bowing fulfills the very dreams they once despised in Genesis 37.

options.text: They recognize Joseph immediately and beg for mercy.
options.note: They do bow, but they do not recognize him; only Joseph knows who they are.

options.text: They are welcomed as honored guests and given a feast.
options.note: That comes later; here Joseph treats them as strangers and accuses them.

options.text: They are turned away without any grain.
options.note: They are not turned away; they are tested and eventually sent home with grain.

quiz.q: Why does Joseph accuse his brothers of being spies and test them?

options.text: To prove their hearts and see whether they have truly changed.
options.note: The testing aims at repentance and restoration, shown by his weeping.

options.text: Mainly to make them suffer as he had suffered.
options.note: There is real pain, but the account moves toward reconciliation, not revenge.

options.text: Because he genuinely believes they are enemy spies.
options.note: He knows exactly who they are; the charge is a deliberate test.

options.text: Because God commanded him to punish them.
options.note: No such command is given; Joseph acts to test and eventually restore them.

quiz.q: How do the brothers interpret the trouble that comes upon them?

options.text: As a reckoning for what they did to their brother long ago.
options.note: Their conscience awakens: surely we are being punished because of our brother.

options.text: As random misfortune from a cruel Egyptian ruler.
options.note: They do feel mistreated, but they trace it back to their own guilt.

options.text: As a test of their trading skills.
options.note: They see something far deeper than commerce, namely God's hand on their sin.

options.text: As proof that they had done nothing wrong.
options.note: The opposite; they openly confess their old guilt to one another.

quiz.q: How is God at work in this chapter?

options.text: Through famine, the journey, and the returned silver, He brings hidden sin to light for healing.
options.note: The brothers sense it: what is this that God has done to us.

options.text: He is mostly absent, letting human schemes run their course.
options.note: God is not named on every line, but His providence clearly drives events.

options.text: He works only to punish and destroy the guilty.
options.note: His aim is restoration, not destruction, as the story will show.

options.text: He has abandoned the family to famine.
options.note: The famine is the very means by which He preserves them alive.

quiz.q: Why does Jacob refuse to send Benjamin to Egypt?

options.text: He fears losing the last son of Rachel and being brought in sorrow to the grave.
options.note: Benjamin is all he feels he has left of Joseph's mother.

options.text: He distrusts the Egyptian ruler's motives entirely.
options.note: There is suspicion, but his deepest reason is grief and fear of loss.

options.text: He believes Simeon will soon be released anyway.
options.note: He shows little hope for Simeon; his focus is on protecting Benjamin.

options.text: He thinks Benjamin is too young to travel.
options.note: The issue is not age but Jacob's fear of losing him as he lost Joseph.

questions: The brothers' old sin surfaced years later in a foreign land. Is there something in your past that God is gently bringing back to mind so it can finally be dealt with?
Joseph tested his brothers to see if they had changed. How can we tell the difference between real repentance and simply being sorry we were caught?
The brothers asked, what is this that God has done to us. Where might God be at work in a hard circumstance you are facing right now?
Joseph held power over those who wronged him yet turned aside to weep. How does his response challenge the way you treat people who have hurt you?
Jacob was gripped by fear of losing Benjamin. Where is fear of loss keeping you from trusting God with someone or something you love?

translationNotes.note: The word rendered silver can also mean money; the same term runs through chapters 42 to 44 as the returned silver keeps unsettling the brothers.
Sheol is the grave or realm of the dead; Jacob pictures his grief carrying him down there, a vivid image of a sorrow he feels he could not survive.
